WBM AET: Oudin vs. Penman-Monteith, validated against OpenET and flux towers

National Park Service Water Balance Model · generated July 27, 2026

This report compares three ways of driving actual evapotranspiration (AET) in the NPS Water Balance Model (WBM): the default Oudin PET method (uncalibrated), a PET-multiplier-calibrated version of Oudin (per-site calibration against OpenET, objective peak_nse), and FAO-56 Penman-Monteith (uncalibrated). All three are validated against two independent references — OpenET (satellite-based remote-sensing ET) and eddy-covariance flux tower ET — across 35 sites spanning five ecosystem types and a wide elevation and climate gradient (2016–2023).

Headline result: calibrated Oudin matches OpenET best at most sites — expected, since it was tuned specifically against OpenET. More tellingly, that same calibration also improves its match to the independent flux tower record (RMSE 56.7 → 46.2 mm/month), so it isn't pure overfitting. Even so, uncalibrated Penman-Monteith is competitive with — and on bias and slope, sometimes better than — calibrated Oudin, despite receiving no site-specific tuning at all.
Read the map with this in mind: calibrated Oudin was optimized site-by-site specifically to match OpenET (notebook 04's PET-multiplier calibration), so its strength in the OpenET comparison below is partly circular, not an independent test. The flux-tower comparison is the fairer read on whether the calibration generalizes.

Methods

The WBM is a daily rain/snow/snowmelt/soil-moisture/AET/runoff model. All three AET variants share identical snow, soil, and runoff parameters, so any difference in AET traces back to the PET method (and, for calibrated Oudin, its per-site multiplier) alone. Oudin PET is a temperature-only formulation with a topographic heat-load/shade adjustment; its calibrated version applies a per-site multiplier optimized against OpenET's 4 km grid-cell ensemble. Penman-Monteith is a full energy-balance method requiring humidity and wind; it returns reference-grass ET (ETo) rather than PET, converted here with a crop coefficient of Kc = 1.0 (a simplifying, uncalibrated baseline). Wind came from gridMET (10 m), corrected to the 2 m height FAO-56 assumes. Penman-Monteith has not been calibrated in this comparison.

Where does each variant do better? (spatial view)

Mapping which of the three variants has the lowest RMSE vs. OpenET at each site shows calibrated Oudin winning almost everywhere (again, expected given how it was tuned) — with uncalibrated Penman-Monteith still taking a cluster of Rocky Mountain sites, and default Oudin winning nowhere outright.

Calibration narrows Oudin's gap to Penman-Monteith in every ecosystem, and overtakes it in Croplands, Grasslands, and Shrublands — but Penman-Monteith (still uncalibrated) remains best in Evergreen Forests and essentially tied in Wetland/Riparian, the two ecosystems where the Kc = 1.0 baseline is least likely to be realistic.

Takeaways

Calibration clearly helps Oudin — and the fact that it also improves the flux-tower match (not just OpenET, which it was tuned against) is a genuine, non-circular result. But the more surprising finding is how well uncalibrated Penman-Monteith holds up against a per-site-calibrated competitor: it has the better slope and bias against both references, even though calibrated Oudin has the lower RMSE against OpenET specifically. That pattern — Penman-Monteith biased less but calibrated Oudin tracking the OpenET target more tightly — is consistent with Penman-Monteith capturing real ET variability (via radiation/humidity/wind) that a per-site multiplier can't fully substitute for. The natural next step is applying the same PET-multiplier calibration to Penman-Monteith, which would make this a fair apples-to-apples comparison instead of calibrated-vs-uncalibrated.
